chunks: And as for what was narrated - Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abu al-Husayn al-Nakha'i from Ibn Abi Umayr from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him):

Regarding a man who hunts game while he is heading to the Sanctuary, and the shot hits him, so he carries it until he enters the Sanctuary and dies in it. He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no penalty upon him; he is in the position of a man who set a net in the open land, game fell into it, struggled until it entered the Sanctuary and died in it.' I said: 'This is considered analogy (qiyas) by them.' He said: 'No, I merely likened one thing to another for you.' This is not contradictory to what we presented earlier, because this report is understood to apply to the one who hunted game in this state, forgetfully or ignorantly, for he does not deserve any punishment for his shot, although redemption (fidya) is incumbent upon him. And his saying (peace be upon him) 'there is no penalty upon him' means no punishment, and this serves as a distinction between the one who hunted game intentionally and the one who hunted it while ignorant or forgetful. What indicates this meaning is what was narrated:

key_terms.الْحِلّ: The open land outside the Sanctuary

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a pilgrim accidentally hit by their own hunting arrow in the Haram?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi uses this narration to demonstrate the distinction between *qiyas* (strict legal analogy) and *tashbih* (descriptive comparison) in Ja'fari jurisprudence, clarifying that the Imam's analogy to a net was illustrative rather than a binding legal derivation. It establishes that accidental hunting incurs *fidya* (redemption) but exempts the pilgrim from *'iqab* (punitive penalty), a ruling applicable whether the error stems from forgetfulness or ignorance. This highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on precise linguistic interpretation over rigid analogical reasoning when deriving rulings from the Imams' statements.
